name: Serer religion
info: The Serer religion, A ƭat Roog, "the way of the Divine", is the original religion of the Serer people of Senegambia in West Africa, centred on the supreme deity Roog, the veneration of ancestral spirits called pangool, and diviner-priests known as Saltigue.

facts.origin: Senegambia in West Africa, among the Serer people, whose ancestors moved south from the Senegal River valley from around the 11th century, with the old Serer kingdom of Sine at its centre; the village of Tukar was founded by Lamane Jegan Joof around the 11th century.
facts.founder: none: the religion is the Serer people's original religion; the founders of Serer villages, the lamane, are remembered as accompanied by the pangool and as the first priests and custodians of the shrines.
facts.scriptures: none written: ancient chants and poems, myths and teachings handed down by Serer priests and elders, including the Serer creation myth.
facts.followers: Most Serers converted to Islam and Christianity after colonisation (about 85% of the Serer people were Muslim by the 1990s), but many still follow the Serer religion, especially in the ancient Kingdom of Sine.

t: Serers believe in a supreme deity, Roog, and address their prayers to the pangool, the ancestral spirits and saints, who are held to carry the prayers of the living to the Divine.
Each Serer family has a totem, the tiim, which is both a prohibition and a guardian: the totem of the Joof family is the antelope, of the Njie the lion, of the Sène the hare.
At the Xooy ceremony the initiated Saltigue, the Serer high priests and priestesses, foretell the coming year before the community at Fatick, in the first week of June.
dyk: Serer spirituality rejects the notion of heaven and hell: a soul accepted by the ancestors may enter Jaaniiw, the place where good souls go, and return to earth through reincarnation, while a rejected soul wanders.
ev: Serers refuse the Muslim leader War Jabi's forced conversion and Sharia law, are defeated, and the first Serer exodus from Tekrur follows
Lamane Jegan Joof founds the village of Tukar, where the Raan festival is held each April; Serers begin to move south from the Senegal River valley
In the Islamic marabout wars, Serers at Naodorou, Kaymor and Ngaye kill themselves rather than be conquered, some jumping into the Well of Tahompa

The funeral rites of the Serer kings are last performed after the death of Maad a Sinig Mahecor Joof, the last king of Sine

sections.origins:
The Serer religion, also called Serer spirituality, is known to its followers as A ƭat Roog, which means "the way of the Divine", "path of God" or "religious life". It is the original set of religious beliefs, practices and teachings of the Serer people of the Senegambia region of West Africa. The ethnologist Simone Kalis writes that it is based on the cult of the ancestors, the pangool, around which all the rituals of religious and therapeutic practice turn. The priest, the o yaal pangool, stands halfway between the world of the beyond and the world here below, between the invisible and the visible, the dead and the living.

Its history is tied to the founding of Serer villages: a group of pangool is said to have accompanied each village founder, called a lamane, the ancient kings, as he travelled in search of land, and the lamane then created shrines to these pangool and became their priests and custodians. The Raan festival is held at the old village of Tukar, founded by Lamane Jegan Joof around the 11th century after he migrated from Lambaye, north of Sine, guided by Saint Luguuñ Joof.

The Serer people are held to have originated in the Senegal River valley, at the border of present-day Senegal and Mauritania, and to have moved south in the 11th and 12th centuries and again in the 15th and 16th. The scholar Dennis Galvan writes that the Serer peoples migrated south from the Fuuta Tooro region beginning around the eleventh century, entering the Siin and Saluum river valleys; the economist Étienne Van de Walle gives a slightly later date, placing the formation of the Serer ethnic group in the thirteenth century. In the late 14th century Mandinka migrants led by the Gelwaar clan entered the area of Sine and met Serers who had already established a system of lamanic authorities.

The Senegambian stone circles, which were probably built by the Serer, were also a place of worship: laterite megaliths were carved, planted and directed towards the sky.
sections.beliefs:
Serers believe in a universal supreme deity, Roog or Rog, sometimes called Roog Sene, "Roog The Immensity" or "The Merciful God", and seen as the embodiment of the male and female. Offerings are made to Roog at the foot of trees such as the baobab, at the sea and rivers, and in people's homes or community shrines. Roog is not the devil nor a genie but the "Lord of creation"; Roog sees, knows and hears everything but does not interfere in the day-to-day affairs of the living, and lesser gods and goddesses act as Roog's assistants. Among them are the fangool Mendiss, a female protector of the Fatick Region, the god Tiurakh, god of wealth, and the god Takhar, god of justice or vengeance.

Ordinary Serers address their prayers to the pangool, the ancestral spirits and saints, who are held to be intermediaries between the living world and the Divine, and prayers are accompanied by ancient songs and sacrifices of a bull, sheep, goat, chicken or harvested crops. The immortality of the soul and reincarnation, ciiɗ, are strongly held beliefs. The righteous, accepted by their ancestors, may enter Jaaniiw, the place where good souls go, and reincarnate; one rejected becomes a lost and wandering soul. Serer spirituality rejects the notion of heaven and hell, and of hell fire. Each family has a totem, the tiim, both a prohibition and a guardian.
sections.texts:
The Serer religion has no written scripture. Its traditional practices include ancient chants and poems, the veneration of and offerings to the pangool, initiation rites, folk medicine, divination, and the preservation of Serer history, culture and identity. The priest, the o yaal pangool, is the master of the cult, and the Serer creation myth belongs to the same oral tradition. Chants are sung when prayers are addressed to the pangool, and Serers also pass on their history and identity through these songs and poems.

The Serer griots have a religious role at the death of a king. On the death of a Serer king, the Fara Lamb Sine, the chief griot of the Kingdom of Sine, buries the king's treasured drum, the junjung, with him; his other drums are played for the last time before being buried in the ground facing east, and the griots chant ancient songs of sadness and praise. The last time this ceremony was held was on 8 March 1969, after the death of the last king of Sine, Maad a Sinig Mahecor Joof.

The Serer cosmos has its symbols. The star Yoonir, which is Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is sacred because it announces the beginning of flooding and lets farmers begin to plant. The Star of Yoonir is also drawn as a sign: its top point stands for Roog and the other four for the cardinal points, and Serers who cannot read or write the Latin alphabet often sign official documents with it.
sections.spread:
The Serer religion belongs to the Serer people of Senegambia, and its later history is one of encounters with Islam and Christianity. Accounts of Serer resistance to Islamisation reach back to the 11th century and the Almoravid movement. By around 1030 to 1035, under the Muslim leader War Jabi, the Serers refused forced conversion and Sharia law; they were defeated, and the first Serer exodus from Tekrur followed, south to where they mixed with the Diola. This exodus affected only the Serers living in Tekrur at the time, not all Serer people.

In the 19th century the Serers fought several prominent African Islamic jihadists. According to the historian James Olson, they "violently resisted the expansion of Islam" by the Wolof, and they were a target of the 1861 jihad led by the Mandinka cleric Ma Ba Jaxoo. Maba Diakhou Bâ, considered a national hero and given saint-like status by Senegambian Muslims, was killed in battle against the Serer king of Sine, Kumba Ndoffene Famak Joof, on 18 July 1867 at the Battle of Fandane-Thiouthioune, commonly called the Battle of Somb. At the surprise attacks on Naodorou, Kaymor and Ngaye, where the Serers were defeated, many villagers killed themselves rather than be conquered by the Muslim forces, among them some who jumped to their deaths at the Well of Tahompa. In Serer religion suicide is permitted only if it satisfies the principle of Jom, honour.

The inter-ethnic wars involving the Serer continued until 1887, when French colonial forces conquered Senegal, and conversion then accelerated. By the early 1910s about 40% of the Serer people had adopted Islam, and by the 1990s about 85% were Muslims. Most Serers converted to Islam and to Roman Catholic Christianity only after colonisation; they and the Jola were the last in the region to convert. Many still follow the Serer religion, especially in the ancient Kingdom of Sine, although Senegal and the Gambia are predominantly Muslim countries. Their long resistance to Islamisation has created a division between "believers" of Islam and "non-believers" such as the orthodox Serers who adhere to the Serer religion. Some Serers syncretise, mixing Islam or Christianity with the old religion.
sections.community:
The Serer are an ethnoreligious group, and the religion is bound up with preserving Serer identity. Endogamy is strongly adhered to: the Serer religion forbids interfaith, interethnic and interracial marriage, and banishment and disinheritance are among the punishments for marrying out. The Serer-Noon, a subgroup, are especially strict about it. Marriage alliances are formed between maternal and paternal clans, and the tokoor, the head of a matriclan, usually its oldest male, tends to arrange marriages. A woman must not be engaged in a physical relationship until marriage, and a couple found in a premarital relationship were both exiled. Adultery is dealt with by the law of compensation, Mbaax Dak A Tiit, and in the past a family could forgive or avenge a killing at a gathering before the chief or king.

Religious life has its own rhythm. Monday is the day of rest and, with Thursday, a day of offerings and libations to the pangool, and Thursday is also a day on which weddings and Senegalese wrestling are prohibited. The Mbeel is the law of charity and hospitality, and the Jom is a code of religious, social, economic, political and ecological values. Men and women may be initiated into the secret order of the Saltigue, which is reserved for a small number of insiders. The dead from the upper ranks of society were mummified and buried in pyramid-shaped tombs with grave goods; mummification is less common now.
sections.legacy:
The Serer religion survives in the practices of its followers and in the ceremonies that gather them. The Xooy ceremony takes place at Fatick, usually beginning in the first week of June, when the Saltigue, the Serer high priests and priestesses, foretell the future in front of the community, including the coming weather, politics and economy. It brings thousands of people to Holy Sine from all over the world, among them Serers who follow only the old religion, Serers who syncretise, and non-Serers such as the Lebou. The Raan festival is held at Tukar every year on the second Thursday after the new moon in April, and some villages of Sine hold an annual rain ceremony, A Cuur Ale.

Serer knowledge of herbalism, passed down over years of learning, is taught at a school and centre set up by the Senegalese government; the CEMETRA, the experimental centre of traditional medicine at Fatick, has at least 550 professional Serer healers as members in Sine-Saloum.

The religion is also held to have left its mark on other faiths of the region. The Serers are one of very few communities in Senegambia, apart from the Jola, whose name for god is not borrowed from Arabic. Senegambian Muslims are said to have taken the names of old Serer festivals, among them Tobaski, Gamo, Korite and Weri Kor, to name Islamic festivals in their own language.

summary: The Serer religion, A ƭat Roog, is the original religion of the Serer people of Senegambia, built on the supreme deity Roog, the veneration of ancestral spirits called pangool, family totems and the divination of the Saltigue priests. The Serers resisted Islamisation from the 11th century to the 19th; most converted to Islam or Christianity after colonisation, but many in the old Kingdom of Sine still follow it.
notes: The saved articles date no beginning for the religion. Start 1000 (circa) is a placeholder resting on the date of Tukar's founding (around the 11th century) and the migration south from the Senegal River valley (around the 11th century); the editor may prefer another.
Removed from the first draft: 1853 and David Boilat (no year in any of the three articles); the 'Raan each April' stays as a recurring festival, not a dated event.

Three sources are in play: the religion article (Tukar, the 1867 battle, the funeral of 1969), the Serer people article (1030-1035 War Jabi, 1861, 1887, early 1910s, 1990s) and the Serer history article (late 14th century Gelwaar). Galvan (11th century) and Van de Walle (13th century) differ on when the Serer ethnic group took shape; both are attributed.

Left out because it conflicts: Serer oral tradition gives 1350 for the first Guelowar king of Sine (Maysa Wali), while the history article puts the Mandinka entry in the late 14th century; neither is used as a key event. The people article says the exodus from Tekrur began around 1030-1035; the history article says it affected only Serers living in Tekrur.

Fewer than five events are not a problem here: seven dated events are supported. The 1861 jihad is dated by the people article (James Olson) only; the 19th-century wars at Naodorou, Kaymor and Ngaye have no year.

Left out: details of the Saltigue's initiation (reserved for insiders); the Serer and Dogon star name claim; remarks about other faiths borrowing festivals; the Battle of Djilass (1859) and Logandème, which are about French colonial rule, not the religion.
Maba Diakhou Bâ's date is 18 July 1867; the Battle of Fandane-Thiouthioune is also called the Battle of Somb.
'Mummification is less common now' and 'buried in a pyramid shaped tomb' are given without dates.
Stone circles: 'probably built by the Serer' per the article, hedged accordingly.
The text uses the article's own spellings: Jaaniiw/Jaaniw, ciiɗ, Saltigue/Saltige, Xooy/Xoy/Khoy.
Faith map: coordinates of Tukar, Fatick, Sine, Tekrur and the battle site are approximate, from general geography.
